blk_explainer_fermentation_foundation.text: Kikkoman soy sauce is a clear example. Soybeans and roasted wheat are combined with koji mold. The koji supplies enzymes that begin breaking down proteins and starches. Salt water is then added to form a mash called moromi. Over several months, microorganisms continue changing this mixture as it ferments and ages. The liquid develops a rich brown color, a salty taste, and a complex aroma.

blk_explainer_cultural_adoption.text: One theory recorded by Japan's Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries links Japanese curry rice to a curry-flavored stew used in the British Royal Navy and later the Japanese Navy during the Meiji era. In Japan, the thick sauce was served over rice with meat and vegetables. Retired sailors helped spread this style to other parts of the country, and curry rice became everyday comfort food. The regional dish known as Yokosuka navy curry keeps that naval connection visible. The words “one theory” matter: food histories often have several routes, not one simple invention story.

blk_explainer_taste_balance.text: People often describe five basic taste qualities: sweet, salty, sour, bitter, and umami. A sauce can add or balance several of them while leaving the food underneath recognizable. Soy sauce gives grilled vegetables or tofu salt and umami. Ketchup gives fried potatoes sweetness and acidity. Mayonnaise adds richness to a dry sandwich or roasted vegetables.
